# Volume 5 — CHAPTER I. HOME AGAIN

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

The May evening was transparent and apple-green, as Seven Gulls Harbour reflected the clouds from the golden west amidst its gently darkened banks. On the sand-bar, the ocean uttered an uncanny mournfulness, melancholic despite the spring, yet a cunning, merry breeze whistled down the crimson harbour road where the cozy, motherly form of Miss Winifred traveled toward the village of Glen St. Agnes. Legally, Miss Winifred was Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, a status she had held for thirteen years, though even now she was called Miss Winifred by more people than called her Mrs. Kerr. Her former name remained cherished by her longtime companions, with a single contemptuous exception. Tabitha Pratt, who served as the gray, austere, and loyal servant to the Carrow household at Hollowmere, seized every chance to address her as “Mrs. Ambrose Kerr,” using the most devastating and deliberate stress, as though implying “You desired to be a Mrs., so a Mrs. you will certainly be to the absolute extreme where I am concerned.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0000 }

Ascending toward Hollowmere, Miss Winifred went to visit Dr. and Mrs. Carrow, who had recently returned from Europe. Their trip had lasted three months, as they had departed in February for the purpose of attending a renowned medical congress in London; furthermore, during the time they were gone, particular events had occurred in the Glen that Miss Winifred was eager to talk about. A new family had settled in the manse, for instance. And what a family they were! Walking at a quick pace, Miss Winifred shook her head about them repeatedly.
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0001 }

As they were seated on the large porch at Hollowmere, taking pleasure in the twilight's magic, the sweet calls of drowsy robins piping amidst the dusk-bound maples, and the flutter of a wind-blown cluster of daffodils swaying near the lawn's aged, soft red brick wall, Tabitha Pratt and the Nell Harcourt of bygone times observed her approaching.
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0002 }

Hands gathered around her knee, Nell sat upon the steps, appearing, within the gentle twilight, as youthful as it is fitting for a mother of numerous children to seem; and her lovely gray-green eyes, which looked along the harbour road, remained as filled with endless glimmer and reverie as always. Resting behind her inside the hammock, Tessa Carrow lay curled, a plump, rotund little child of six years who was the youngest among the Hollowmere children. Her hair was red and curly, and her hazel eyes were currently shut tight in the amusing, crinkled manner that Tessa constantly fell asleep in.
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0003 }

Harcourt, whom the family “Who’s Who” referred to as “the little brown boy,” lay sleeping held in Tabitha’s arms. His hair was brown, his eyes were brown, and his skin was brown, featuring extremely rosy cheeks, and Tabitha cherished him above all others. Nell suffered a prolonged, severe illness following his delivery, prompting Tabitha to care for the infant as a mother with an intense affection that had not been awakened by any of her other beloved children. Indeed, Dr. Carrow had stated that his survival would have been impossible without her.
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0004 }

“Mrs. Dr. dear, I brought him into this world every bit as much as you,” Tabitha was accustomed to remarking. “The baby belongs to me every bit as much as he belongs to you.” Furthermore, Harcourt would invariably race to Tabitha whenever he needed his bruises kissed better, to be swayed into slumber, and to be shielded from earned beatings. Every one of the remaining Carrow offspring had been dutifully thrashed by Tabitha whenever she believed their spiritual well-being required it, yet Harcourt was spared her hand, nor would she permit his own mother to strike him. On one occasion when Dr. Carrow inflicted a spanking upon him, Tabitha reacted with furious rage.
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0005 }

“Sweet Mrs. Dr., that fellow would whip a seraph, he surely would,” she had asserted with venom; and for many weeks, she refused to bake a pie for the unfortunate doctor.
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0006 }

She had brought Harcourt along to her brother’s residence while his mother and father were away, whereas every other child had departed for Brierley, granting her three glorious months with him entirely on her own. Even so, Tabitha was delighted to return to Hollowmere and be surrounded by all her beloved ones once more. Hollowmere constituted her universe, a realm where her authority was absolute. Even Nell rarely disputed her judgments, which deeply irritated Mrs. Agatha Sowerby of Grey Shutters, who dismal-fashion informed Nell, on every occasion she went to Seven Gulls, “you are letting Tabitha get to be entirely too much of a boss and will live to rue it.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0007 }

“Winifred Tolley is walking up the harbour road right now, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha remarked. “She will be arriving here to dump three months’ worth of gossip upon us.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0008 }

“I hope so,” said Nell, embracing her knees. “I’m dying for Glen St. Agnes gossip, Tabitha. I hope Miss Winifred can inform me about all that has taken place during our absence—everything—who has been born, or married, or drunk; who has died, or departed, or arrived, or fought, or lost a cow, or found a beau. It’s so wonderful to be back home with all the beloved Glen folks, and I want to hear everything about them. Why, I recall wondering, while I was strolling through Westminster Abbey which of her two particular suitors Millicent Drew would ultimately marry. Do you know, Tabitha, I have a terrible feeling that I love gossip.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0009 }

“Well, of course, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha admitted, “any proper woman enjoys listening to the news. I myself am somewhat interested in Millicent Drew’s situation. I was never had by a beau, let alone two, and it does not bother me now, because being an old maid fails to hurt once you grow accustomed to it. To me, Millicent’s hair constantly appears as though she swept it up using a broom. Nevertheless, the men appear not to mind it.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0010 }

“Only her attractive, charming, sarcastic, small face is visible to them, Tabitha.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0011 }

“That could indeed be true, Mrs. Dr. dear. It is stated in the Good Book that favor is deceitful and beauty is vain, yet I would not have objected to discovering that personally, had it been so destined. Undoubtedly, every one of us will be beautiful once we become angels, but what benefit will that bring us at that point? Turning to the subject of gossip, though, it is reportedly said that over harbour, poor Mrs. Pettifer Miller attempted to hang herself last week.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0012 }

“Oh, Tabitha!”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0013 }

“Compose yourself, Mrs. Dr. dear. Her attempt failed. Yet I cannot truly fault her for attempting it, since the man she married is a dreadful person. Nevertheless, she acted quite foolishly in considering hanging herself, which would only make room for him to wed a different woman. Had I found myself in her situation, Mrs. Dr. dear, my approach would have been to badger him until he attempted to hang himself rather than me. This is not to say that I approve of anyone hanging themselves in any situation, Mrs. Dr. dear.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0014 }

“Anyway, what is wrong with Pettifer Miller?” Nell asked with impatience. “He constantly forces somebody into taking drastic measures.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0015 }

“Indeed, a few individuals label it religion whereas others term it cussedness, asking your forgiveness, Mrs. Dr. dear, for employing such phrasing. It appears they are unable to discern which one applies regarding Pettifer. On certain days he snaps at everyone owing to his belief that he is predestined for everlasting damnation. On other days, however, he claims he remains indifferent and proceeds to become intoxicated. In my personal view, his mind lacks soundness, given that no members of that Miller family line possessed sound minds. His grandfather lost his sanity. He believed large black spiders encircled him. They crept across his body and drifted through the atmosphere around him. It is my wish that I never become mad, Mrs. Dr. dear, and I doubt I shall, since such behavior is not characteristic of the Bakers. Nevertheless, should a supreme Providence ordain it, I pray it does not manifest as large black spiders, because I detest those creatures. Regarding Mrs. Miller, I remain uncertain if she truly merits sympathy or not. Certain people claim she wedded Pettifer solely to anger Richard Taylor, which strikes me as an exceedingly strange motive for wedlock. Yet, naturally, I lack the authority to evaluate marital matters, Mrs. Dr. dear. Look, Winifred Tolley stands by the gate, meaning I shall place this dear brown infant upon his mattress and retrieve my knitting.”
{: #nw-v05-c01-p0016 }
